m1-t1.question: According to the lesson, what is the decisive difference between digital marketing and traditional marketing?
options: Digital marketing reaches younger audiences than hoardings or print
Almost everything in digital marketing can be measured, so it can be improved and defended
Digital marketing does not require any budget to start
Traditional marketing cannot create awareness for a brand
m1-t1.explanation: The lesson defines digital marketing as attract–convert–keep, measurably: measurement is what lets you improve campaigns and justify spend.

m1-t1.question: A small café's WhatsApp broadcast list of regular customers is an example of which kind of media?
options: Paid media, because sending messages consumes budget
Earned media, because customers opted in voluntarily
Owned media, because the business controls the list and it costs nothing per use
Shared media, because it exists on a phone
m1-t1.explanation: Owned media — website, blog, email/WhatsApp lists — is fully controlled by the business and compounds without per-use cost.

m1-t1.question: Which statement best describes how the channels in a healthy marketing plan relate?
options: Each channel should be judged independently, and the weakest one cut
Channels assist each other: social finds winning messages, paid amplifies them, content receives the traffic, email retains it
Paid media should be used only after all other channels have failed
Search, social and email target different customers and should never overlap
m1-t1.explanation: The lesson's pattern: channels do not compete, they assist — each stage of the journey is served by a different channel's strengths.

m1-t1.question: Why does the lesson call a plan that runs only on paid media 'renting growth'?
options: Because ad platforms charge commissions on every sale
Because paid media stops delivering the moment spending stops, unlike owned and earned assets that keep working
Because paid media cannot be measured accurately
Because paid ads are always more expensive than hoardings
m1-t1.explanation: Paid media is instant but rented; owned (site, list) and earned (rankings, reviews) assets keep paying after the spend ends.

m1-t1.question: A café gets more morning orders after setting up a Google Business Profile, a WhatsApp combo broadcast and small search ads. What did the student actually change?
options: The café's pricing and menu
The café's location advantage
The system: matching channels to where customers already are, each with a measurable job
The café's staff training
m1-t1.explanation: Same café and same tools — the shift was from random activity to a measured system where each channel has a job.

m1-t2.question: In the funnel arithmetic 1000 visitors × 3% enquiry × 40% qualified × 25% close, how many customers result?
m1-t2.explanation: 1000 × 0.03 = 30 enquiries; × 0.40 = 12 qualified; × 0.25 = 3 customers. Funnel maths is honest multiplication.

m1-t2.question: A customer reading comparison articles and reviews is in which stage, and what are they really asking?
options: Awareness — 'does this exist?'
Consideration — 'is this right for me, and better than the others?'
Conversion — 'is it safe to go ahead?'
Advocacy — 'should I tell others?'
m1-t2.explanation: Consideration is the comparison stage; the customer's question is fit and relative superiority, served by honest proof.

m1-t2.question: Traffic is healthy but almost nobody fills the enquiry form. What does the lesson say to do first?
options: Buy more traffic to compensate for the low rate
Switch the whole budget to television
Diagnose and fix the conversion-stage leak before buying more traffic
Post more frequently on social media
m1-t2.explanation: Do not pour more traffic into a leaky funnel: fixing a 1% → 2% conversion rate doubles results at zero extra spend.

m1-t2.question: Cost per acquisition (CPA) must be judged against which other number?
options: The campaign's total budget
The number of impressions served
The customer's lifetime value (LTV)
The competitor's ad spend
m1-t2.explanation: CPA below customer lifetime value is a good trade; the same CPA can be profitable for one business and ruinous for another.

m1-t2.question: Which channel pairing is correctly matched to its home funnel stage?
options: Search ads on high-intent keywords → awareness
Email journeys to existing customers → retention
Reels and influencer content → conversion
Retargeting ads → awareness
m1-t2.explanation: Email and messaging own retention and advocacy; search ads convert existing intent; social and influencers build awareness.

m1-t3.question: Why does the lesson call imagined personas 'a mirror'?
options: Because they must be reviewed every quarter
Because they usually describe the marketer's assumptions rather than the actual customer
Because customers change their minds too often
Because every persona needs a photo to feel real
m1-t3.explanation: Imagination-based personas reflect the writer's guesses; evidence-based personas are built from search data, reviews, listening and interviews.

m1-t3.question: You want to find market gaps for a new tutoring service. What does the lesson suggest reading first?
options: The 5-star reviews of the market leader, for inspiration
The competitor's 'About us' page
The 1–3 star reviews of competitors, because every complaint is a market gap
The competitor's follower count on Instagram
m1-t3.explanation: Low-star reviews are the cheapest research goldmine: each recurring complaint is a gap you can own.

m1-t3.question: Which persona field does the lesson say actually changes marketing decisions?
options: The persona's name and age
The persona's favourite colour
Triggers and barriers — what makes them start looking and what stops them buying
The stock photo chosen for the persona
m1-t3.explanation: Situation, goals and fears, watering holes, triggers and barriers, and proof that moves them — the fields that change what you write and spend.

m1-t3.question: In interviews, why does the lesson forbid 'would you be interested in…?' questions?
options: They are too long to ask in ten minutes
People politely say yes to hypotheticals; asking about the last real instance gets the truth
They only work on social media
Because surveys are always better than interviews
m1-t3.explanation: Hypothetical interest is social politeness; 'tell me about the last time you…' reconstructs real behaviour.

m1-t3.question: What can you learn from the Meta Ad Library that you cannot see on a competitor's public page?
options: Their employee count
The paid messages they are actively running right now
Their annual revenue
Their customer personas
m1-t3.explanation: The Ad Library shows every active ad a brand runs — the messaging they are willing to pay for, not just what they post organically.

m1-t4.question: Which goal passes the SMART test?
options: Increase brand awareness for the campus store
Get more engagement on our posts
Get 300 of the college's 2,400 students to use WhatsApp ordering before the November exams at under ₹40 per first order
Become the most popular store on campus
m1-t4.explanation: Number + audience + channel + deadline + efficiency line: a stranger could verify success on the deadline date.

m1-t4.question: In a KPI tree, what is the role of diagnostic metrics like opens and scroll depth?
options: They are the numbers the budget is defended with
They explain why a KPI moved, but do not drive decisions on their own
They replace KPIs when baselines are missing
They are reported only to the finance team
m1-t4.explanation: KPIs drive decisions; diagnostics explain them. Confusing the two is how dashboards fill with noise.

m1-t4.question: The goal is admissions, but the enquiry-to-admission rate is weak. What does the KPI tree suggest is the likely right move?
options: Immediately double the ad budget
Shift spend and effort to follow-up quality and CRM discipline instead of more awareness
Stop all marketing until the rate improves
Report only reach and impressions to the client
m1-t4.explanation: Reading the whole tree tells you where the constraint is; buying more traffic into a weak conversion stage wastes money.

m1-t4.question: Why is the 'out of scope' line the most underrated part of a one-page brief?
options: It makes the brief look professional to investors
It is how professionals say no without conflict and keep a two-week project two weeks long
It is required by the DPDP Act
It lists the KPIs the client cares about
m1-t4.explanation: Explicit exclusions prevent scope creep — every line you do not exclude will arrive at your door by week two.

m1-t4.question: A brief sets a target of 800 marketing-sourced enquiries with no record of how many enquiries came last month. What is missing?
options: The message
The baseline — without today's number you can never prove you moved it
The audience
The channel mix
m1-t4.explanation: Baselines can be rough estimates, but they cannot be missing: no baseline means no provable result.

questions.question: A boutique spends ₹30,000 on ads, gets 2,000 visitors, 80 enquiries and 10 customers. A customer spends ₹6,000 and typically returns twice a year. What is the honest verdict?
options: Profitable: CPA ₹3,000 is below the ₹6,000 first purchase
Unprofitable: 2,000 visitors is too few to judge
Profitable only if the customer returns — CPA ₹3,000 against ₹12,000 annual value makes it a strong trade
Impossible to judge without knowing the click-through rate
questions.explanation: CPA = 30,000 ÷ 10 = ₹3,000. With repeat purchases the customer's value compounds; the funnel arithmetic and LTV together justify the spend.

questions.question: A dental clinic's website gets 1,500 visits a month, a 4% call-button click rate, but only 1 in 12 callers books. Where is the constraint, and what is the first fix?
options: Awareness — the clinic should buy more ads immediately
Conversion-to-booking — the leak is at the front desk / follow-up; script, response speed and reminder flow come before more traffic
Consideration — the website needs more blog articles
The clinic should switch from ads to hoardings
questions.explanation: Traffic and click intent are healthy; the bottleneck is the human follow-up stage. Fix the leak before buying more traffic.

questions.question: Which set contains ONLY KPIs (decision-driving numbers) for a goal of '300 WhatsApp first-orders by November'?
options: First orders, cost per first order, share of orders from WhatsApp vs walk-in
Followers, impressions, story views
Page likes, post reach, hashtag uses
Number of posts published, hours spent, photos taken
questions.explanation: KPIs connect to the goal and its economics; followers and impressions are diagnostics that explain, not decide.

questions.question: Reading a competitor's 5-star reviews, you notice the words 'patient' and 'explained everything' appear constantly; 2-star reviews of other competitors say 'rushed'. What is the gap sentence?
options: Everyone says quality, so we should also say quality louder
Everyone rushes, nobody promises patience and clear explanations — so we will make 'we take time to explain' the lead promise and prove it
We should copy the competitor's pricing
Reviews are unreliable and should be ignored in research
questions.explanation: The gap sentence names the shared cliché, the silence in the market, and your ownership of it — built directly from review evidence.

questions.question: A team's persona says 'likes fitness and Instagram' but their sign-ups are flat. Their interviews revealed timing clashes and class-WhatsApp as the real channel. What did the original persona violate?
options: The rule that personas need photos
Evidence-based construction — the persona was imagination, so the campaign targeted the wrong barrier and the wrong watering hole
The requirement to survey at least 100 people
Nothing; the campaign just needed more budget
questions.explanation: The campaign failed on barrier ('not fitness people') and channel (WhatsApp groups) — both fields a persona must capture from evidence.

questions.question: Which situation is 'always-on marketing' rather than a campaign?
options: A Diwali discount week with a fixed start and end date
A one-time product-launch burst with a dedicated budget
A claimed Google Business Profile, weekly newsletter and community replies that run every week
A two-week admissions push with a deadline
questions.explanation: Always-on marketing compounds quietly every day; campaigns are focused bursts with a goal and an end date. Healthy brands run both.

questions.question: Your KPI tree shows 800 enquiries needed for 120 admissions (15% conversion), but the current rate is 10%. Which re-forecast is consistent with the tree?
options: Keep the 800 target and accept 120 admissions
Either raise enquiries to 1,200 at the current 10%, or lift the conversion rate to 15% through counselling quality
Reduce the goal to 80 admissions and report success
Move the entire budget to brand awareness
questions.explanation: The tree makes the two honest levers visible: more enquiries at the same rate, or a better rate on the same enquiries — the second is usually cheaper.

questions.question: A business owner says: 'Our customers are everyone in the city.' What is the professionally correct first response?
options: Agree and design a broad awareness campaign
Ask for evidence: autocomplete phrases, low-star reviews of competitors, and five ten-minute customer interviews before choosing a target
Start paid ads and let the data decide later
Build a persona with a name, age and photo first
questions.explanation: The four evidence sources — search data, reviews, listening, interviews — turn 'everyone' into a targetable audience with real barriers and watering holes.

questions.question: During a campaign, reach doubles but orders stay flat. Which interpretation fits the lesson?
options: The campaign is working; orders will follow eventually
Reach is an awareness-stage diagnostic — the constraint is further down the funnel, so audit consideration and conversion stages next
The audience must be expanded further
The metric tool is broken
questions.explanation: When a top-of-funnel diagnostic moves but the outcome does not, the constraint lives in a later stage — that is what the tree is for.

questions.question: Which brief line most reliably prevents a two-week project from becoming two months?
options: 'Channels: we will use all of them'
'Out of scope: no logo redesign, no website rebuild, no offline events'
'Goal: maximise engagement across platforms'
'Budget: as needed'
questions.explanation: Explicit exclusions are how professionals say no without conflict — scope creep arrives through every door left open.
